Marilyn Monroe (Marilyn), shocking pink colourway

One of Andy Warhol’s ten 1967 Marilyn screenprints: a publicity photograph reduced to black, laid over flat blocks of hot pink, yellow, and peach.

Source
V&A: Marilyn Monroe (Marilyn), CIRC.123-1968
Creator
Andy Warhol
Made
1967
Style
Pop art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Brash, glamorous, commercial
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, CIRC.123-1968 (1200 × 1198 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A records a screenprint on paper, 91.4 × 91.6 cm, printed by Aetna Silkscreen Products Inc./Du-Art Displays and published by Factory Additions, New York, 1967. The print is one of a portfolio of ten colourways; this one is described as shocking pink, yellow, and peach. V&A.

The V&A notes that every print and painting Warhol made of Marilyn used the same publicity photograph by Gene Kornman for the 1953 film Niagara. V&A.

The painted version of the motif is Marilyn Diptych.

Observed

  • The background is a flat hot pink that fills the square to the edges.
  • The hair is a flat yellow shape; the face is a flat peach shape with no modeling.
  • A black screen of the photograph gives the eyes, brows, nose, mouth, and the shadowed side of the face and neck.
  • Eyelids are a brighter pink block, and the lips are dark red under the black.
  • The color blocks do not align exactly with the black layer: the yellow runs past the hair outline at the right edge.

Why it belongs

Warhol replaces the drawn key line with a black photographic layer, and the process primaries with a hotter palette. The style record’s Warhol variant comes from works like this.

The misregistration is part of the look: flat color and line are two separate layers that do not quite meet.

Borrow

For a Warhol variant, set a black high-contrast image over flat blocks of hot pink, yellow, and peach.

Offset one color block a few pixels from the black layer to suggest a printing misregister.
